The safest advice is to visit a running store and get fitted. Some argue that a runner is fine regardless of the pronation support in their shoes; some live by the belief that you should be fitted to get the support that is right for you. Either way, I think it's safe to say that high quality running shoes are a good investment as they can help decrease fatigue and reduce injuries.

I am similarly built as you (6', 200lbs), and I've been battling injuries for a while (stress fracture in foot, metatarsalgia, mild plantar fasciitis). I've recently switched over to Hokas and have been very happy. I was reluctant to make the change because of just how huge they look, but now I don't think I'll go back to my asics.

I second everything you've said. Your shoes should be the one thing you don't cheap out on in running. Your feet take such a pounding during a run, and all that force translates up through your shins, your knees, and your hips. A lot can go wrong through all of those biomechanical linkages; getting a correct fitting shoe for your stride, foot shape, etc. can really make a difference.

Purely anecdotal, but after wearing through my first shoe, I tried a second brand/line. I went from half-marathon distances to not being able to run a 5k due to foot pain...getting the right shoe can make all the difference in the world.
